explanation:
## The three signatures say everything

```rust
fn measure(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() }        // borrows
fn shout(mut s: String) -> String { ...; s }       // takes and returns
fn consume(s: String) -> usize { s.len() }         // takes
```

In Rust the signature is a contract about **ownership**, not just about types,
and the compiler enforces it at every call site. Read `&String` as "I will look
at yours" and `String` as "give me yours".

## What a move actually is

```rust
let loud = shout(word);
```

At runtime this copies three machine words - a pointer to the heap buffer, a
length and a capacity - from `word` into the parameter. The heap buffer is not
copied. That is the same thing a C++ move does.

The difference is what happens next. Rust marks `word` as moved-from at **compile
time** and refuses to let you read it:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `word`
```

Not a warning, not a runtime check - the program does not build. And because
`word` can never be read again, Rust also knows not to run its destructor, so
the buffer is freed exactly once, by whoever owns it at the end.

Compare the C++ equivalent:

```cpp
std::string word = "cache";
std::string loud = std::move(word);
std::cout << word;            // legal, compiles, prints... something
```

After a `std::move`, the source is in a *valid but unspecified* state. Reading it
is well defined behaviour that gives you an unspecified value - in practice an
empty string with every major implementation, which is exactly why the bug
survives code review. Rust makes the same operation a compile error.

## Why `shout` has to give it back

```rust
fn shout(mut s: String) -> String {
    s.make_ascii_uppercase();
    s
}
```

`shout` takes ownership, so when it returns, `s` would be dropped and the
buffer freed - unless it hands ownership on. Returning `s` does exactly that:
the three words are moved into the caller's `loud`, and no destructor runs.

That `mut` in `mut s: String` is worth a second look. It is **not** part of the
parameter's type - the caller does not need a mutable `word`, and the type is
still `String`. It says the binding inside the function body is mutable. You own
the value now, so whether you mutate it is your business.

This take-and-return shape is common in Rust for exactly this reason. The
alternative is to borrow mutably:

```rust
fn shout_in_place(s: &mut String) { s.make_ascii_uppercase(); }
let mut word = ...;
shout_in_place(&mut word);          // word still belongs to the caller
```

which is what you would usually write, and what the next problem is about.

## Two borrows at once are fine

```rust
let n = measure(&word);
let m = measure(&word);
```

Any number of shared references can exist simultaneously, because none of them
can modify anything. The restriction is on `&mut`, which must be the only
reference alive - that is the next problem.

Note that `&word` is a `&String` here, which is slightly unidiomatic. Most Rust
code would write:

```rust
fn measure(s: &str) -> usize { s.len() }
```

because `&str` accepts both a borrowed `String` (through deref coercion) and a
string literal, so the function is usable in more places for free. This problem
asks for `&String` so that the borrow is explicit in the type while you are
learning what it means.

## `len()` counts bytes

```rust
"cache".len()      // 5
"café".len()       // 5 - four characters, five bytes
```

A Rust `String` is guaranteed-valid UTF-8, and `len()` is the length of its byte
representation. For ASCII the two coincide, which is why the statement pins
input to ASCII. For anything else you want:

```rust
word.chars().count()          // Unicode scalar values - O(n), not O(1)
```

and `chars().count()` is still not "characters as a person would count them",
because an emoji with a skin-tone modifier is several scalar values. Rust makes
this visible by refusing to let you index a string with `word[0]` at all - there
is no cheap, correct answer to "the first character", so the language declines
to pretend otherwise.

`make_ascii_uppercase` is named the way it is for the same honesty: it changes
`a-z` and nothing else, in place, without reallocating - because a general
Unicode uppercase can change the byte length (German `ß` becomes `SS`) and so
cannot be done in place at all.

## Why ownership instead of a garbage collector

Rust frees a value when its owner goes out of scope, which the compiler knows
statically. So there is no runtime tracking, no reference counting on every
assignment, no collector pauses - and no way to free twice, use after free, or
leak through a dangling pointer. The cost is paid entirely at compile time, in
the form of this problem's error messages.

That is the trade C++ cannot make, because its moves are a library convention
rather than a language rule: `std::move` is just a cast, the source object stays
usable, and the compiler has no basis on which to object.
